## Problem1

```{r p1_function}
simulate_birthday = function(group_size) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = group_size, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}
```
```{r p1_simulation}
set.seed(1)

birthday_results =
  tibble(group_size = 2:50) |>
  mutate(
    shared_birthday = map(
      group_size,
      \(n) map_lgl(
        seq_len(10000),
        \(iteration) simulate_birthday(group_size = n)
      )
    ),
    probability = map_dbl(shared_birthday, mean)
  )


```
```{r p1_plot}
birthday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "#0072B2") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2, 10, 20, 23, 30, 40, 50)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Shared birthdays become more likely as the group grows",
    subtitle = "10,000 simulated groups at each group size",
    x = "Number of people in the group",
    y = "Probability of at least one shared birthday"
  )
```

For each group size, I averaged the results of 10,000 simulations. The estimated probability of a shared birthday is `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * birthday_results$probability[birthday_results$group_size == 23])` for 23 people and `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * birthday_results$probability[birthday_results$group_size == 50])` for 50 people. The probability rises quickly because the number of pairs of people increases with group size. A group of 23 people already contains 253 possible pairs, so a shared birthday is fairly likely even though there are 365 possible birthdays.

## Problem2
```{r p2_import}
subject_files =
  tibble(
    file_path = list.files(
      "data",
      pattern = "^(con|exp)_[0-9]{2}\\.csv$",
      full.names = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    file_name = basename(file_path),
    data = map(
      file_path,
      \(path) read_csv(
        path,
        col_types = cols(.default = col_double()),
        show_col_types = FALSE
      )
    )
  )

```

```{r p2_tidy}
study_df =
  subject_files |>
  select(file_name, data) |>
  unnest(cols = data) |>
  mutate(participant_id = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$")) |>
  separate(
    participant_id,
    into = c("arm", "subject_id"),
    sep = "_",
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    arm = factor(
      arm,
      levels = c("con", "exp"),
      labels = c("Control", "Experimental")
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  select(participant_id, subject_id, arm, week, observation) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)


```

I first created a dataframe of file names and used `map()` to read each participant's observations into a list column. I then expanded the list column, extracted the arm and subject ID, and converted the eight weekly columns to long format. The tidy dataset contains `r nrow(study_df)` observations from `r n_distinct(study_df$participant_id)` participants followed for eight weeks. Each row represents one participant at one week. Subject IDs are repeated across arms, so `participant_id` combines the arm and subject ID to identify each person uniquely.

```{r p2_summary}
arm_summary =
  study_df |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(
    participants = n_distinct(participant_id),
    week_1_mean = mean(observation[week == 1]),
    week_8_mean = mean(observation[week == 8]),
    mean_change = week_8_mean - week_1_mean,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

```{r p2_plot}
study_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = participant_id,
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.75, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Control = "#0072B2", Experimental = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly observations for each participant",
    subtitle = "Each line follows one participant; panels use the same y scale",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observed value"
  )
```

The experimental group shows an overall upward pattern, while observations in the control group fluctuate around a more stable level. The experimental group mean increases from `r sprintf("%.2f", arm_summary$week_1_mean[arm_summary$arm == "Experimental"])` in week 1 to `r sprintf("%.2f", arm_summary$week_8_mean[arm_summary$arm == "Experimental"])` in week 8. The corresponding control group means are `r sprintf("%.2f", arm_summary$week_1_mean[arm_summary$arm == "Control"])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", arm_summary$week_8_mean[arm_summary$arm == "Control"])`. Individual trajectories vary in both groups, but the separation between groups is clearer by the later weeks.

## Problem3
```{r p3_function}
simulate_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
  x = rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

  t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided") |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(mu_hat = estimate, p_value = p.value)
}
```

```{r p3_simulation}
set.seed(3)

simulation_results =
  tibble(true_mu = 0:6) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(
      true_mu,
      \(mu_value) tibble(iteration = seq_len(5000)) |>
        mutate(
          result = map(
            iteration,
            \(i) simulate_t_test(mu = mu_value)
          )
        ) |>
        unnest(cols = result)
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = results) |>
  mutate(rejected = p_value < 0.05)
```

```{r p3_summary}
simulation_summary =
  simulation_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarise(
    rejection_rate = mean(rejected),
    mean_estimate = mean(mu_hat),
    mean_estimate_rejected = mean(mu_hat[rejected]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

```{r p3_power_plot}
simulation_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = rejection_rate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#0072B2") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Power increases as the true mean moves away from zero",
    subtitle = "Two-sided one-sample t-tests; n = 30, SD = 5, alpha = 0.05",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests rejecting the null",
    caption = "At a true mean of zero, the rejection rate estimates the Type I error rate."
  )
```

With the sample size and standard deviation fixed, power increases as the true mean moves farther from zero. The estimated power is `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * simulation_summary$rejection_rate[simulation_summary$true_mu == 1])` at a true mean of 1, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * simulation_summary$rejection_rate[simulation_summary$true_mu == 2])` at a true mean of 2, and `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * simulation_summary$rejection_rate[simulation_summary$true_mu == 4])` at a true mean of 4. Larger effects are easier to distinguish from sampling variability. At a true mean of zero, the null hypothesis is true, so the rejection rate of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * simulation_summary$rejection_rate[simulation_summary$true_mu == 0])` estimates the Type I error rate, which is close to the chosen 5% significance level.

```{r p3_estimate_plot}
estimate_plot_df =
  simulation_summary |>
  select(true_mu, mean_estimate, mean_estimate_rejected) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mean_estimate, mean_estimate_rejected),
    names_to = "sample_set",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sample_set = factor(
      sample_set,
      levels = c("mean_estimate", "mean_estimate_rejected"),
      labels = c("All samples", "Rejected tests only")
    )
  )

estimate_plot_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = average_estimate, color = sample_set)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("All samples" = "#0072B2", "Rejected tests only" = "#D55E00")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Selecting rejected tests changes the average estimate",
    subtitle = "Dashed line: average estimate equals the true mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = NULL
  )
```

Across all samples, the average estimated mean is close to the true mean. Among rejected tests, the average estimate is higher than the true mean when the true effect is small and positive. For example, at a true mean of 1, the average estimate is `r sprintf("%.2f", simulation_summary$mean_estimate[simulation_summary$true_mu == 1])` across all samples and `r sprintf("%.2f", simulation_summary$mean_estimate_rejected[simulation_summary$true_mu == 1])` among rejected tests. Rejection depends on the sample mean relative to its estimated standard error. When the true positive effect is small, samples with unusually large positive means are more likely to pass the rejection threshold, so retaining only rejected tests inflates the average estimate. As power approaches one, almost all samples are retained and the two averages converge.

At a true mean of zero, the two-sided test selects extreme means in both directions. Symmetry makes the conditional mean zero in expectation, even though the selected estimates tend to be farther from zero. In this finite simulation, the average estimate among rejected tests is `r sprintf("%.4f", simulation_summary$mean_estimate_rejected[simulation_summary$true_mu == 0])`; its departure from zero reflects Monte Carlo variability.
